name: Turkmenistan
summary: A desert country rich in natural gas; Soviet until 1991; one of the most closed states in the world.

location.value: Central Asia; about 491,000 km²; mostly Karakum Desert.

terrain.value: About four-fifths is the flat Karakum Desert; the Kopet Dag mountains run along the Iranian border, and the Amu Darya river flows in the east.

climate.value: Very dry continental desert climate: hot summers often above 40 °C, cold winters and little rain in most places.

resources.value: Natural gas reserves among the four largest in the world, including the giant Galkynysh field, plus oil, sulphur and irrigated cotton land.

disasters.value: Earthquakes (the 1948 Ashgabat earthquake killed tens of thousands), and salty soils and the shrinking Aral Sea caused by heavy irrigation.

population.value: Official figures say about 7 million, but outside estimates are lower and reliable data are scarce.

urbanisation.value: About half the people live in towns; the capital Ashgabat is the largest city, followed by Türkmenabat, Daşoguz and Mary.

disease.value: Reliable health data are scarce; the government reported no COVID-19 cases, which outside health experts doubted.

migration.value: Many people, especially young adults, have left to work or study in Russia and Turkey, though leaving is often restricted by the authorities.

economicBase.value: Natural gas exports, mainly to China, plus oil, state-controlled cotton and wheat farming, and construction.

tradeRoutes.value: The Central Asia–China gas pipeline (opened 2009) carries gas east; gas also goes to Russia and Iran, and the Caspian port of Türkmenbaşy links west.

wealth.value: Gas income pays for showcase building in Ashgabat, but official statistics are unreliable and many rural people remain poor.

moneyAndTax.value: The manat, introduced in 1993 and redenominated in 2009; most state income comes from gas sold by state companies.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

keyRulers.value: Saparmurat Niyazov. Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow. Serdar Berdimuhamedow.

succession.value: Presidents are chosen in elections that outside observers have not judged free; in 2022 the presidency passed from father to son.

institutions.value: A powerful presidency with a weak parliament (the Mejlis), state-run media and a strong personality cult around the president.

stability.value: Few open political conflicts since 1991, but rights groups describe tight state control and little room for opposition.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: Small armed forces equipped mainly with Soviet-era weapons; under its neutrality policy the country joins no military alliances.

majorWars.value: No wars since independence; it stayed neutral during the wars in neighbouring Afghanistan.

territoryChange.value: No changes: its borders are those of the former Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic, set up in 1924.

alliancesRivals.value: Recognised by the UN as permanently neutral (December 1995); only an associate member of the CIS, it balances ties with Russia, China and Iran.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Schooling was cut to nine years in the 1990s and higher education shrank; reforms from 2007 restored ten-year and later twelve-year schooling.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Soviet-era railways plus new lines such as the Kazakhstan–Turkmenistan–Iran railway (2014); internet access is tightly restricted.

religion.value: Mostly Sunni Muslim (about 90%), with a Russian Orthodox minority; religious groups must register with the state.

languageWriting.value: Turkmen, a Turkic language, switched from Cyrillic to a Latin alphabet in 1993; Russian is still used.

artsArchitecture.value: Ashgabat’s white marble buildings, the Ertuğrul Gazi Mosque, traditional hand-knotted carpets and Akhal-Teke horse culture.

socialStructure.value: About 85% Turkmen, with Uzbek and Russian minorities; tribal origins such as Teke, Yomut and Ersari still matter socially.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity built on the Turkmen language, tribes, carpets and horses, promoted by the state since 1991.

dailyLife.value: Many families live in Soviet-era flats or village houses; plov (rice pilaf), bread baked in tandyr ovens and green tea are everyday food.

ideasReligions.value: The Ruhnama (2001), a book of history and moral guidance by President Saparmurat Niyazov, was compulsory in schools until after his death in 2006.

colonisation.value: Part of the Russian Empire from the 1800s and the Soviet Union from the 1920s until 1991.

riseSignals.value: Declared independence from the Soviet Union on 27 October 1991 as the USSR broke up.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; gas exports to China from 2009 brought its largest income.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still an independent country, with the same borders and capital (Ashgabat) as at independence in 1991.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
